userJob: Decide what to build as a section and what to hardcode in a Shopify theme
problem: A page is built as one fixed template, so the client cannot reorder or remove anything and every later change is a developer task
worksWhen: Any Shopify theme build where the merchant will maintain the page after handover
avoidWhen: A structural element that must not move, such as the acquire control on a product template, where editability is a liability
mechanism: Build page composition as sections with a schema, and let the JSON template decide which sections a page has and in what order. Anything you hardcode outside a section is invisible to the merchant. Decide per element which of the two it is, and write that decision into the direction record so handover is not a surprise.
risks: Making everything editable, so the merchant can reorder the page into a state that breaks the design's argument
Setting section limits and presets carelessly, so the merchant can add ten of something meant to appear once
mobileRules: A merchant-reordered page has to hold at 375px in any order the schema permits, which is a constraint on the schema rather than on the CSS
accessibilityRules: Heading level cannot be assumed when section order is editable; derive it or set it per section rather than hardcoding a single h2 everywhere
genericnessNote: Section-based composition is the platform's own shape, so the difference between two Shopify sites is what the sections contain rather than that they exist.

userJob: Expose the design's values so the merchant edits them in the theme editor rather than in code
problem: Colours and type are written directly into stylesheets, so the merchant's theme editor still offers its own controls and changing them does nothing, or changes half the site
worksWhen: Any Shopify theme intended for handover
avoidWhen: A value that must never change, which belongs in code precisely so it is not offered as a control
mechanism: Declare the direction's values as theme settings and render them into custom properties from one place in the layout, then reference those properties everywhere. Name the settings after the subject's own materials rather than as generic slots, because the setting name is what the merchant reads when deciding what to change.
risks: Two sources of truth, where a setting exists and the stylesheet ignores it, so the control appears to be broken
Exposing so many settings that the merchant can produce a combination that fails contrast
mobileRules: A merchant-set value applies at every width, so any responsive scale derived from it has to hold across the whole permitted range
accessibilityRules: Any colour pair the settings allow has to clear 4.5:1, not only the pair you shipped
Document the contrast constraint next to the setting, because the merchant is the one who will break it
genericnessNote: Generic setting names are how a direction reverts after handover, so the naming carries more weight here than in a stack with no editor.

userJob: Design a purchase path when part of it is outside the theme
problem: The design is planned end to end, and then checkout turns out to be a hosted surface the theme cannot restyle, so the commitment moment looks like a different company
worksWhen: Every Shopify commerce build, at plan time rather than at the end
avoidWhen: Never; discovering the boundary late is the expensive version of discovering it
mechanism: Establish where the theme stops before planning the purchase path. Cart is usually yours. Checkout is a platform surface with its own limited customisation, which depends on the merchant's plan. Design the commitment so the whole commitment is legible before the reader crosses the boundary, and treat the crossing as a deliberate, stated moment rather than a seam.
risks: Building brand identity that only exists up to the boundary, so the last step reads as a redirect to somewhere else
Assuming a customisation is available without checking what the merchant's plan permits
mobileRules: The boundary is most visible at 375px, where the change in type and spacing fills the screen
accessibilityRules: The hosted surface has its own accessibility behaviour that you neither control nor may claim; test it and report what you found rather than assuming
genericnessNote: The boundary is a platform fact, and what it forces is a decision about where the design's argument has to land.

userJob: Build product templates against data that already exists rather than data you wish existed
problem: A template is designed around fields the catalogue does not have, so at launch every product shows empty specifications or a placeholder where the design's best element was
worksWhen: Any product, collection or listing template on a real catalogue
avoidWhen: A demonstration build with invented products, which is a different job and should be labelled as one
mechanism: Read the real catalogue before designing the template. Establish which fields are populated for all products, which for some, and which do not exist. Design the guaranteed fields into the structure and treat the partial ones as optional branches with a defined empty state. Missing structured data is a request to the merchant, not something the template invents.
risks: Designing around a field only the sample product has
Filling a missing field with a plausible value, which is a claim about the merchant's product
mobileRules: Optional branches change the stack height at 375px; check the template with the sparsest real product, not the richest
accessibilityRules: An optional block that renders empty leaves an unlabelled region; render nothing rather than an empty container
genericnessNote: Designing from the real catalogue produces a template shaped by this merchant's data.

userJob: Render product images and prices the way the platform expects
problem: Images are referenced at their original size and prices are formatted by hand, so pages ship oversized files and a store in another currency shows a wrong-looking figure
worksWhen: Any theme rendering product images or prices, which is all of them
avoidWhen: A static asset that is part of the design rather than the catalogue, which is yours to size and serve
mechanism: Request catalogue images at the sizes the layout actually uses and let the platform serve them, with width and height declared so nothing shifts. Format money through the store's own money filters so currency and locale follow the merchant's settings rather than your assumption.
risks: A hand-formatted price that is correct in the development store and wrong in every other market
Serving the original upload, which is usually several times the size the layout needs
mobileRules: Request the mobile size separately rather than serving the desktop asset to a 375px slot
Declare the aspect ratio on every image so the collection grid does not shift as it loads
accessibilityRules: Alt text comes from the merchant's own image alt field where it exists; falling back to the product title repeats the heading and says nothing
genericnessNote: Asset and money handling are platform mechanics with no design content.
